#308. The Best Automatic Litter Box of 2026: Petkit and Litter-Robot

I can confidently say that having an automatic litter box has been the biggest game changer for me when it comes to cat ownership. I can't recommend them enough. They can be pricey, but never having to scoop poop again is priceless.

We at WIRED—well, our WIRED cats—tested a dozen of the highest-rated and most technologically advanced automatic litter boxes on the market for at least a week, often more (using standard clay clumping litter unless otherwise indicated), to see if they were really worth the money—or the hype. Our new favorite automatic litter box is the Purobot Max Pro 2 because of its compact design and camera for monitoring. The Litter-Robot 4 is a close second, mostly because of its LitterHopper attachment that easily refills litter for you. Plus, we still love the more basic Petkit PuraMax 2 (and think it's a great option for most people).

Check out our related guides, like the Best Automatic Feeders, Best Cat Water Fountains, Best Pet Cameras, and Best Cat Toys. More of a dog person? We've got you covered; see our Best Dog Accessories.

Updated September 2026: We've added the PetPivot AutoScooper 12 and Whisker Litter-Robot EVO, and updated links and prices throughout.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

The Purobot Max Pro 2 is the newest model from Petkit. It features a built-in 1080p camera with a 210-degree wide-angle view. The AI-enabled camera supports multi-cat face recognition, usage tracking (via a companion app), audio recording, night vision, and 2.4-GHz and 5.0-GHz Wi-Fi networks. The camera can also record video of the cat using the box and of their stool or urine.

This model has a 43 percent larger opening than the previous one, the PuraMax Pro, making it ideal for large cats like my 16-pound tabby, Basil. The waste bag is also larger: It stores up to 17 days of waste for one cat and is self-sealing for easy disposal. The Petkit app sends an alert when the waste basket is full, and two odor-eliminator cartridges help keep odors at bay.

You get Petkit's premium Care+ service for a free trial period. It detects unusual activity, like howling; logs weight and use frequency; and sends an alert if your cat’s weight shows a consistent increase or decrease (a great way to monitor your cat's overall health). When Care+ ended, it still could tell my cats apart, but reviewer Kat Merck and others have complained that it got their cats confused. Petkit's app still could use some work to be more intuitive, and it's overcrowded with ads. Overall, though, my cats took to this right away (which isn't always the case), and even my large cat was able to use this automatic litter box easily. I'm still not sure we need to be watching our cats defecate, but it is an incredible way to monitor your pets' health more closely.

I've tested over 30 automatic litter boxes, but I still go back to this old model from Whisker. This previous model of the Litter-Robot (the new Litter-Robot 5 line was released in fall 2025; see our thoughts about the new 5 Pro, 5, and EVO models below) has been a consistent favorite, largely due to its well-designed app and auto-refill Hopper (more on that below). Unlike Petkit, which has great automatic litter boxes with subpar apps that are crowded with ads for other products in the brand's lineup, the Whisker app (available for Android and iOS) is simple and intuitive. It logs usage and weight daily and historically, and it monitors litter and waste levels, alerting you when either is low. You can also adjust things like lights, manually start cycles, and set “Do Not Disturb” schedules so it won't cycle during certain periods.

After continued testing, it sometimes senses ghost cats and stops repeatedly during cleaning cycles, and alerts that the waste drawer is full when it's barely 20 percent filled. But this remains a favorite and a top pick, in part because of the super-convenient optional LitterHopper auto-refill attachment, which acts as a clean litter resivoir and refills litter to perfect levels. No more bending, scooping, or pouring clean litter multiple times a week! Without the attachment, I think Petkit's new model (our current top pick) is the best automatic litter box for most people, but I still think Litter-Robot is a great choice (and is the model I use at home with my cats) because of the connected app and LitterHopper auto-refill attachment.

This is a great option for most people—cheaper than some of our other picks, easy to use, and compact. Perhaps best of all, when it's time to refill with clean litter, the box rotates so the hole is on top for easier filling. Not only does this litter box smell neutral, dare I say it smells … good? This box has triple odor control: a sealed waste bin, an odor-eliminator attachment that sits in the waste bin, and a citrusy deodorizing spray that goes off after every cleaning and randomly throughout the day to ensure the litter box stays fresh. When the cat enters the box, their weight is displayed on the front, and the app logs every time it is used, for how long, when the cleaning cycle begins and ends, and when the deodorizing spray was deployed. Owners can also change settings manually via the buttons on the front.

My only complaints are that the app could be better—it's overcrowded with ads for other Petkit products, and unlike the Litter-Robot 4, the box doesn’t have sensors to tell you when the litter’s low or needs to be refilled—that has to be manually checked (or you can add manual reminders via the app). One of my cats, who is 17 pounds, didn't like using it as much because the opening was cramped for him, so if you have bigger cats, this may be a problem.

This automatic litter box uses a style very similar to many on the market, and after testing several disappointing boxes in a row, I was pleasantly surprised by this one. Set up took less than five minutes—all you need to do is pop on the legs, insert a liner and the waste drawer below, insert a deodorization cartridge, and connect to the app. Through the connected app, you can schedule cleanings, clean on demand, empty the litter, enable “sleep” mode, adjust the cleaning delay, and switch device settings such as child lock, indicator lights, and beeping.

The litter box worked without issue during testing, and my cats took to it easily. However, like others on the market, the app is poorly translated into English, and some of the controls and directions were a bit confusingly worded. And because of the wide-open-top design, my cats tended to kick out and track litter much more than with more contained designs like the Litter-Robot. I ended up vacuuming daily, so if you choose it, I highly recommend getting a large tracking litter mat beneath it. Overall, though, I’d recommend this model if you’re only looking to spend a few hundred bucks and you want a connected app to better monitor your cat's habits and health. Plus, Lesure is giving away free automatic litter boxes to bodega cats in NYC! We have to stan.

The Whisker Litter Robot EVO was super simple to set up, though its box is absolutely gargantuan. It was basically a plug-and-play experience, with an intuitive app and a large, sealed waste drawer that keeps odors in. The box itself is streamlined and a good option for apartments or smaller rooms compared to other boxes I’ve tried. It took up basically the same amount of room as a standard litter box—it’s just taller. My only complaint is that my box didn’t come with waste drawer liners, and I have yet to find an inexpensive dupe on Amazon. These are OK, but not perfect. (The box is supposed to come with waste drawer liners, just FYI). The EVO is a shorter, more compact, pared-down version of the pricier Litter-Robot 5 and Litter-Robot Pro, offering support for up to two cats weighing up to 19 pounds each.

I have to empty the drawer about once per week, which is an easy process. The Litter Robot 5 and 5 Pro can go up to 10 days between drawer emptying, but for me, once per week for my single-cat household has been completely manageable and an extra three days wouldn't make a noticeable difference in terms of convenience. I have noticed that sometimes, waste can get stuck to the “ceiling” of the box, but that’s a rarity and can happen with any box, and it's also easy to correct with a scoop or paper towel. All in all, my cat took to this robot box quickly, it’s easy to clean, it has virtually no odors, it’s basically silent, and the app keeps me informed with zero issues. It’s easy to recommend for a one- or two-cat household, especially if you don’t need bells and whistles like automatic litter level sensing and AI waste identification. I like that it's relatively simple (which is also why it's more affordable).

The app lets me know when the drawer is close to full, keeps me posted on cleaning cycle trends like how many scoops I've saved, and measures my cat's weight, but there's no AI or cameras or extra nonsense that I likely wouldn't find useful. I haven't used the Whisker+ subscription, partially because its paid features include things like facial recognition and WasteID, which the EVO doesn't support anyway. Overall, this robot litter box is minimal compared to its more expensive siblings, which is a blessing in my opinion. If you want extra accessory compatibility, AI tools, a night-light, or automatic litter refills, this box will be too simple. But if you just want something that'll scoop for you and help you keep an eye on the frequency of use and your cat's weight, or you want a smaller footprint than some other boxes, I like the EVO a lot. It offers the Litter Robot convenience with a smaller price tag and a more streamlined experience. If you care more about accessory compatibility, or have multiple cats or big cats, the Litter Robot 5 or 5 Pro may be better options. —Louryn Strampe

There’s a lot that I like about this automatic device from Homerunpet. It’s huge, with a 106-liter capacity (and holds 8 liters of litter, plus a 4.5-liter reservoir), making it ideal for big, chonky cats weighing up to 20 pounds (or multiple-cat households). My cat gets claustrophobic in most domed boxes, and she used this one right away. I like that it dumps and refills its own litter, and that it has anti-pinch sensors and two escape routes that are always open. There’s a drawer for storing the waste bags that line the poop drawer, as well as underneath the box, so you can dump all the litter at once. It cleaned itself efficiently and quietly.

One thing to note is that the box is absolutely massive upon arrival—I couldn’t fit it in the back seat of my Mazda 3—and the litter box itself is huge, with a frustratingly short cord that might make placement inconvenient. My other gripe was with the app, which had some poorly translated instructions and alerts that sometimes left me feeling confused. But if you’re the proud parent of a hefty feline, it’s still an option worth considering, especially with its 90-day trial—you can return the box for a full refund if you pay the return shipping fees. —Louryn Strampe

PetPivot AutoScooper 12 for $200: This is a good automatic litter box for this super-low price point, and if your budget is $200, this is so much better than a traditional box. However, I still think the picks above are the cream of the crop. This is the new-and-improved version of the 11 model below. It doesn’t have a connected app, which I don't love because I like to track my cat’s weight and usage, and I like being able to adjust settings from afar. But if you’re looking for a more hands-off model without much maintenance, a simpler, budget box like this may be a good option. Setup was super easy—all you need to do is put the included waste bags in the bin, attach the top, pop on the feet and ramp, and fill the litter. It’s on an automated timer and starts cleaning about four minutes after it senses the cat has left, but you can also do a manual cleaning and litter leveling through the buttons on the outside of the machine. PetPivot claims that it can hold waste for up to 10 days without needing to empty, but I found that the bottom waste drawer (which is less enclosed than other models I’ve tested) started smelling like wet sewage after a few days and needed more frequent emptying. There’s also no option to set different times for cleaning after usage, and often small litter clumps from urine would stick to the grate because it didn’t have enough time to solidify. There’s also no option to completely empty the litter in settings, which made it difficult (and messy) when I wanted to deep clean and when donating. My main gripe is that my cats kicked out so much litter during use due to the low, open-top design. If you go with this model, be sure to use litter tracking mats or have a vacuum cleaner on standby.

PetPiviot Autoscooper 11 for $170: This automatic litter box doesn’t have all the bells and whistles of some others on this list, but if you’re looking for a basic, inexpensive automatic box, I’d recommend this one. It has an open-top design that remains fully open throughout the cleaning cycle and has sensors to know when the cat has used the box and when or if the cat reenters during the cleaning cycle. Like most others, it spins dirty litter from clean using grates, and the dirty litter is deposited in a drawer below the box. The litter box is the smallest and lightest I’ve tested, and the only assembly required was popping on the legs and inserting the drawer (and putting a waste bag liner in). There’s no app required for use, and functions can be controlled by three buttons on the box—clean, refill litter, and power on/off. When you want to completely empty the litter, you attach a plastic cover that pops on to scoot all of the litter into the drawer below. Since this has no app, you won’t be able to closely monitor your cats’ usage or get alerted when the drawer is full, so this requires more check-ins than other WIRED-tested automatic boxes on this list.

Whisker Litter-Robot 5 Pro for $899: This model is part of Whisker's newest Litter-Robot lineup, which also includes the mid-level Litter-Robot 5 and the base-level EVO. It has an AI-enabled camera that can recognize up to five cats and WasteID technology to determine what type of visit your cat had—the only model I've tested with this capability. The dual-camera system captures external motion outside the box and inside the litter bed. It also charts trends over time to help you more accurately understand your cats' health and habits, so you know if anything is amiss. Plus, depending on the type of waste, LR5 Pro gives more targeted odor control, cycling immediately for solid waste and waiting for urine to make sure it clumps. The drawer is also more sealed and larger, with up to 10 days of waste storage per cat. It looks similar to my personal favorite auto box, the Litter-Robot 4 (above), but has a built-in camera, a touchscreen rather than physical buttons, a wider and shallower drawer, and a taller (removable) lip in the entryway. Maybe I'm just partial to the older model, but I think all of these changes make it less user-friendly than the 4 model. The touchscreen is finicky, the drawer liners are harder to place perfectly with the shallow design, and the removable entryway lip is much harder to attach and detach with smaller insertion tabs that feel like they could break off. Setup took several days because onboarding requires scanning a QR code with the built-in camera, but the camera never auto-captured the code. It'd be much easier if you could enter the code manually rather than relying on the camera. The camera always panned to the outside of the box rather than inside, and rarely showed footage of the stool/pee. Plus, the AI to differentiate cats only works reliably with the Whisker+ paid subscription plan ($80/year).

Petkit Purobot Ultra for $800: I liked this automatic box a lot, even if some of the features are a little over the top. (Read the full review here.) It uses a camera and AI technology to monitor litter box usage and lets you see your cat’s stool to help you more closely monitor their health. This upgrade has a large horizontal footprint and a camera on an arm in front of the opening, which swivels and follows your cat when it senses motion and records inside the litter box (it also has night vision). It has auto-bagging and -sealing features, so you never have to deal with the stool. The app logs and monitors usage, including the number of times used and the average duration. The camera has 180-degree viewing, two-way audio, and 24/7 streaming. It uses AI to identify which cat used the box, and while it doesn’t explicitly note whether a cat peed or pooped, you can review the footage to determine. Although this is a good idea in theory, the videos inside the litter box aren’t hi-def and are always in black-and-white, which makes it very difficult to actually observe anything in detail. The arm’s placement is awkward, making it extremely challenging to refill the litter box. This litter box always worked well and kept smells at bay, but the AI analytics fell a little flat for me, and it was needlessly tough to refill the litter.

Litter-Robot 5 for $799: The middle model Litter-Robot 5 offers several improvements and design tweaks over the base Litter-Robot 4: easier assembly and waste removal; an LCD screen; and, if you have a Whisker+ subscription, a new WasteID feature that is supposed to distinguish between feces and urine. This only worked intermittently in the first four months of testing, as did the LR’s ability to tell my cats apart by their weights. However, the firmware on the 5 was recently updated and has improved greatly over time, with fewer error codes and more consistent WasteID readings. I very much prefer Litter-Robot’s larger opening to Petkit’s, the ease of cleaning, and the fact it can hold 10 days' worth of waste from my two cats before needing to be emptied. It's also a step up from the base-level EVO in that it can accommodate five cats up to 30 pounds. I highly recommend adding on Litter-Robot's new ramp ($75) and litter-trap mat ($50), either of which helps to cut down on litter tracking, but both together resulted in a significant reduction in how often I had to vacuum. —Kat Merck

Petcove PurrTek Covered Self-Cleaning Litter Box for $360: I was surprised when my two large cats easily took to this very small automatic litter box. I wasn’t even sure my 16-pound cat would be able to fit inside. Set up was super easy: Just insert the step (my cats preferred to use it without because they’re so large and it took up valuable real estate inside), plug in, download the connected app, and connect the box to Wi-Fi. The waste bag was already installed, and there were also large buttons on the front to manually control settings like auto- or manual-cleaning, deodorization, auto-leveling, waste or litter emptying, and sensing. I’ve grown to really appreciate easy outside buttons, which are a game-changer when the often buggy app crashes or you aren’t near your phone. Like many automatic litter boxes I test, this product would be vastly improved with a better app interface and clearer English translations. It was very hard to figure out what the settings were asking or even if they were set, mostly because of the poor translation. Waste bin calibration could be set from zero to 15, and litter leveling setting could be set from zero to six, seemingly arbitrary numbers that didn’t seem to change settings. “Do not disturb” mode could be set, but only for a specific clock time, such as 11:30 pm, rather than a time span, which wasn't useful. It also took an egregiously long time to sift the waste, at almost four and a half minutes for the whole cycle. I wish the waste bin were at the bottom of the device, because emptying and refilling the bag was often messy and had litter leakage. The device worked without issue overall, and my cats liked it, but for almost $400, I’d get the Petkit PuraMax 2, which fluctuates at a similar price but works so much better.

Els Pet Orbitie for $300: This is one of the least expensive automatic litter boxes, but it functions much like the more expensive models, with an internal 65-liter-capacity orb that rotates and catches clumps with a plastic grate, depositing them into a bag-lined box below. The opening is a generous 12 by 12 inches—plenty big enough for my two 8-year-old cats, who took to it almost immediately despite never having seen anything but a traditional litter box. The accompanying Orbitie app doesn’t offer an extensive amount of information; it tells the user the volume of litter and what step of the cleaning phase the box is currently in, as well as how many times the box has been used and at what times. The first test unit I received was faulty—it sent multiple phantom alerts to the app, letting me know it had cleaned itself as many as 36 times a day, which I knew for a fact was not true. The replacement unit, however, works just as intended, though the bin beneath fills up fast (about every other day with my two cats), and it needs to be disassembled and cleaned every month or so, as tiny pieces of cat litter have a tendency to get in the gears beneath the orb and make a loud grinding noise. Online reviews panned an earlier version of this box, but Orbitie says this is an improved version. Thankfully, like the bigger brands, Orbitie also offers a 90-day money-back guarantee if you’re on the fence. —Kat Merck

FurryTail Automatic Litter Box Pro for $250: I was surprised by how quickly and easily my cats took to this device—even my larger cat, who hates change, started using it right away. Setup was super easy, and the box comes with a year's supply of waste bag liners, an additional grate attachment, and a mat to reduce litter tracking. Similar to many models, the spherical orb rotates, sifting dirty litter into a waste bag, which, on this model, is on top of the machine rather than below. The box has both a manual display and buttons on the machine, as well as an app to adjust settings. I'd include this model in our top picks because of how easy it was to set up and use, as well as how much my cats liked it, but the app was basically useless. Through the app, you can adjust settings like timed cleanings and do-not-disturb modes, manually clean, and monitor waste levels. However, the app never tracked usage or weight, and for the majority of the time, didn't clean when I manually instructed it to. The sensors would sense ghost cats and refuse to clean, with the device not automatically cycling for the majority of the day (which sort of defeats the purpose). This automatic box has tons of potential, but I can't fully recommend it until the kinks (especially in the app) are ironed out.

Casa Leo Leo's Loo Too Automatic Litter Box for $650: This automatic litter box was a top pick for a long time, but it's pricey and a bit cramped for some cats. We still like it, but think the options above are better for most people (and cats). There are four weight sensors inside the barrel to detect when a cat is still inside (it needs just 1 pound of weight to detect your cat), an anti-pinch sensor (for fingers and paws), and a radar system that detects when anyone, feline or human, is near it. For extra cleanliness, it also uses ultraviolet light for extra sanitation. The Smarty Pear app alerts you when the drawer is full (about once a week), records the times your cat uses it and the cat's weight, and you can set it to automatically clean six seconds to 20 minutes after your cat uses it. You can start a cleaning session manually from the app or use your voice if you connect the box to Alexa or Google Assistant. Former WIRED reviewer Medea Giordano’s biggest struggle using the Loo Too was pouring new litter into it, which can be tricky because of the small entry hole. The barrel is also pretty cramped, especially for her 12-pound cat.

PetSafe ScoopFree SmartSpin Self-Cleaning Litter Box for $350: This basic automatic litter box is around half the price but has a similar design to more expensive models. This futuristic-looking pod on legs has a rubbery bottom, a weight detector that sets off the cleaning cycle a few minutes after your cat has done its business, and a slide-out tray in the bottom. After they’ve been, the body rotates, and a mesh catches the clumps and deposits them in the tray, where there’s a bag with a wee deodorizer unit that smells like watermelon. You can connect it to Wi-Fi and review your cat’s toilet visits in the app on your phone, where each entry displays the time they went, their weight, and toilet trip duration. This self-cleaning box was easy to build and works surprisingly well, even though it feels kinda cheap. Ultimately, as a relatively affordable self-cleaning device, the PetSafe ScoopFree SmartSpin is worth a look. —Simon Hill

Petlibro Luma Smart Litter Box for $600: I'm a big fan of Petlibro's automatic feeders and fountains, but I've found that the brand's other tech products, like this automatic litter box and AI-enabled pet camera, aren't on the same level. First, we cannot recommend any model that closes completely during cleaning cycles. The Luma is outfitted with tons of sensors to prevent cleaning while a cat (or any object) is inside or near the entrance, and I highly doubt injury would occur. But the globe spins backward and forward, rather than clockwise and counterclockwise, meaning that the entrance is closed during cycling. If a sensing malfunction happened, the cat would be trapped inside. I appreciated the button controls on the outside top, which allow for manual control. However, they're on a touchscreen above the camera. So, oftentimes, when I tried to manually reset, the camera caught me and wouldn't continue the cleaning or control I asked of it, because the safety features would prevent action inside the box. It was very frustrating. When I went out of town, it got stuck in the middle of the cleaning cycle for two days because it kept sensing a ghost cat. The globe was mid-cycle, and the entrance was covered; I couldn't bypass via the app to keep cleaning. (Thank God I had a second litter box for my cats available, or I would've been out of luck.) The auto-deodorizing feature goes off automatically for five minutes after each use and sounds like an airplane engine. There's no way to turn it off; you can turn the power down to a lower level, but it's still egregiously loud. Right now, I can't recommend this model (mostly for safety reasons), but a lot of the design flaws could be fixed in future iterations to make it a solid choice.

Oneisall Ease S1 Self-Cleaning Litter Box for $230: Full disclosure: I tested this in a beta version before it was released to the public, so I hope my major complaints have been fixed in later manufactured models. This automatic box is constructed from hygienic stainless steel to keep things cleaner and less prone to harboring odors, it has a simple design, and it’s affordable. I’m generally a fan of Oneisall’s pet tech; I’ve been impressed by various models of the brand's simple, affordable automatic pet fountains and automatic pet feeders. This model is also super simple, with a few front-facing buttons to control settings and no connected app. On the front is the status light, which will flash different colors for things like waste basket full, improper installation, and motion detection. It has buttons for turning off manual or auto-cleaning modes and leveling litter. For the first five days of “testing,” the automatic box detected a cat and stayed perpetually in cleaning mode. No matter what buttons I pressed, there was no way to override or reset it; even when I unplugged and replugged, the cleaning cycle would continue without end. When leveling litter, it would sense a ghost cat and stay perpetually in a wonky position for hours, if not days. Once it eventually went into standby mode, the litter wasn’t flat, and the box was slightly angled. My cats were too freaked out to use it regularly because it was always moving or at an odd angle. I love that it’s affordable, simple, and has hygienic stainless-steel construction, but some serious design changes need to be made—primarily a way to override ghost sensing to complete a cleaning cycle, and perhaps a connected app—before I can recommend this model.

PetSnowy Snow+ Self-Cleaning Litter Box for $530: This box looks like something from Kubrick’s visions of space travel, or if Eames started making plastic litter boxes. It takes up quite a bit of horizontal floor space, so it may not be ideal for those in cramped apartments looking to conserve space. Unlike all others on this list, this globe is closed during cleaning, which could cause injury if the machine malfunctioned and didn’t sense a cat. The box also doesn’t tell you when the litter’s low or needs to be refilled. My cats had a really hard time using it—they just couldn’t understand that it was a litter box. Older cats could have a tough time jumping into it, and the smaller opening could be a problem if you have bigger cats. It might be great for someone who wants to keep things tidy—it’s extremely clean, smells good, and hugely reduces litter tracking. However, we just can't recommend the device since it's closed during cleaning, which is not safe.

The Pet Zone Smart Scoop for $166: This is probably the least “smart” automatic litter box we've tested—it's a typical rectangular plastic box with an automatic arm that acts as a rake and scoops the clumped (soiled) litter into a small bin on the other side. Once the cat leaves, it begins a 15-minute countdown and the rake slides over the length of the box, (ideally) scooping up the waste and lifting it into the receptacle. You’re only allowed to fill the device with about an inch and a half of litter, which my cats didn’t like (they prefer a few inches to really bury it). The rake doesn’t stop when it's in the cleaning cycle—even if something jumps in, which is potentially dangerous. My cats tend to pee on the side of the litter box, which, because of the rake’s placement, means it misses an inch on either side—I still had to scrape the caked-on litter from the edges. The cycle timing can’t be adjusted, so the litter didn’t have time to clump completely, and the rake would immediately break it down into smaller clumps that would then be missed because they were too small. For me, the hassle's not worth it, and I’d rather just scoop it myself.

Automatic litter boxes vary depending on the brand and litter type. Generally, they have sensors, either by motion or weight, to tell when a cat has entered or exited the device. Usually customizable and controlled via app on your phone, or on a more rudimentary timer system, the cleaning cycle will begin a short time after the cat has used the box. With dome-shaped litter boxes, the cleaning will happen via a cycle where the litter spins and rotates around the spherical interior; the bigger soiled clumps will be deposited into the waste basket while the clean granules pass through the grates and get recycled back into the box.

The Petkit PuraMax 2, for example, rotates backward and then forward (rather than a clock-wise/counter-clockwise spin cycle) to sift the clumps from the clean litter, depositing the larger clumps into the waste basket. The Pet Zone Smart Scoop is the most rudimentary design we tested, simply using a rake attachment to scoop the bigger clumps into a waste receptacle in the back.

Pet owners should always do research and make an informed decision regarding which box is best for them and their cat. We only tested automatic litter boxes that remain open during cycling to ensure that if for some reason the weight sensors didn't pick up on a cat being inside, the cat could jump out. We don’t recommend devices that close completely because of the potential that the machine could not sense the cat and kill it during its automatic cycle.

These automatic boxes use sensors—some only needing 1 pound of weight to detect your cat—where the cycle will automatically stop no matter where it is in the cleaning process. Many also have anti-pinch sensors. For added security, the devices on this list have customizable schedules, including “do not disturb” modes. If you're a neurotic helicopter cat mom like me, you could only run the clean cycles when you choose, like when you're in the room to observe the cycle (although if you do that, the box won't stay clean for as long).

Where Should I Put the Automatic Litter Box?

All of these automatic litter boxes require electricity, so they will need to be near an outlet. Since cats will generally take a little while to get comfortable with their new potty, I recommend that you keep your old litter box until they use the device regularly. It helps to put the new automatic litter box near the old boxes to familiarize your cat with it. Adding in litter attractant and using old litter from the previous box also encourages your cat to use the new model.

As a general rule, for old-school litter boxes, you should have one box for each cat, plus one. With automatic models constantly cleaning, there is less need for multiple options, but we recommend leaving your old litter box out for an extended period to ensure the cat has acclimated to the new automatic box.

After testing around a dozen automatic litter boxes, I look for several things that make day-to-day life with the device easier for you and your pet. First, the connected app. This is what you'll be checking daily, so it's important that it works well. This is one of the reasons the Litter-Robot 4 was our top pick for a long time: its connected app is intuitive, simple to use, and reliable. I absolutely love the Petkit models we've tested, but the app is subpar, overcrowded with ads for other products and poorly translated. I also look for anything that makes filling litter easier: I love the Litter-Hopper attachment, which refills litter for you on Litter-Robot models, the self-filling litter reservoir on Homerunpet, and the self-sealing waste bags of the newest Petkit models. You'll also want to keep the cat's size in mind. My two cats are large, so I tend to opt for something with an extra-large, front-facing hole. Which box you choose depends on litter type and compatibility—if you're using tofu litter, make sure you get a model that is compatible with your preferred type. Budget is also a factor, with some models as low as $150 or as high as nearly a grand.

How Does WIRED Select Models to Be Reviewed?

I do a lot of research, looking up other reviews online, including our competitors, to see which are getting buzz. Since I'm the pet tech writer here at WIRED, I also have knowledge from other pet tech brands I love for things like automatic feeders and pet water fountains. Most of these brands also have automatic litter boxes, which I always try to test among their lineup of new pet tech. I also talk to other cat-parents to see what they're using (and liking). I aim to test a wide range of styles and price points for every type of budget and cat.

Sometimes we reach out to brands we're excited about and receive samples for potential review; other times we will buy a model we're interested in and expense it.

What Does WIRED Do With Them After Testing?

We keep some models on hand for long-term testing to see if they hold up over time. This is especially useful for our former top pick, the Litter-Robot 4, whose Litter-Hopper attachment eventually stopped working, or the Petkit models, whose AI starts falling flat without a Care+ subscription. Keeping some devices for longer-term testing helps ensure that we are giving our readers a comprehensive review. Most boxes we test for several weeks and donate locally upon completion.

Rudimentary automatic litter boxes have been around since the late ’80s. These early models featured an automatic rake attachment (much like the Pet Zone Smart Scoop box) but had problems with reliability and loudness. It wasn’t until the 2010s that the devices started incorporating advanced tech like Wi-Fi and app control. In the decade since, that technology has continuously grown and improved, with most devices providing insight into your cats’ habits and health—truly becoming an asset in understanding your feline friends even better.

My cats are currently testing the Petkit Purobot Max 3, the newest model in beloved brand Petkit's automatic litter box lineup; and the Bissell CleanWell Self Cleaning Litter Box, the first automatic litter box model in the cleaning titan's new pet tech category.

#307. Sony's MDR-3R wired headphones are steeped in retro aesthetics

This is actually a refresh of a model that dates back to 1979.

Everything old is new again. Sony just announced a refresh of its iconic MDR-3 wired headphones, which go all the way back to 1979 and accompanied the very first Walkman portable tape player.

The MDR-3R headphones look extremely similar to the source material, though the earpads are available in two unique colorways. This is a retro experience through and through — the headphones are wired, with no option for wireless connectivity.

There are a couple of modern features. First of all, these connect via USB-C and not a 3.5mm headphone jack. They also boast a built-in microphone for phone calls, which certainly didn't exist in 1979, and a volume knob.

Otherwise, these are very light and simple wired headphones. They should get the job done, though will likely pale in comparison to a high-end pair of studio cans. They do look pretty cool though.

There are two versions available here. The standard MDR-3R headphones ship with blue and orange earpads and cost $60. Weirdly, there's also a version based on the Netflix show Stranger Things, which ended its run last year. These are essentially the same, but feature a Stranger Things logo on the headband and black and red earpads. They are also more expensive, at $80. Both models are available right now.

This is just the latest product that hints at a retro resurgence, as many people seem to be tired of some aspects of modern tech. Simple digital typewriters are on the rise, as are boomboxes and other cassette players. Instant cameras are getting pretty big again and so are old-school flip phones. Even RadioShack is making a big bet on retro tech as part of its comeback plan.

#303. US judge temporarily blocks Trump's arch project after panel approval

A judge ordered a two-week stop to construction on US President Trump's arch project in Washington. A federal panel had approved Trump's triumphal arch plans in an 8-4 vote.

A United States federal judge on Friday blocked President Donald Trump's administration from breaking ground on a proposed 250-foot (76-meter) memorial arch for two weeks, shortly after it won a key approval from a public commission.

The temporary restraining order comes as a setback for one of the most prominent projects in Trump's vision to remake the US capital to his tastes.

The Trump administration claims that Congress approved the construction of a monument at the site more than 100 years ago. But that plan envisioned two large columns, signifying the northern states and the southern states in the US Civil War — not an arch.

"The sheer improbability ​that a 100-year-old statute would contain authority, unknown to every previous administration, to erect a 250-foot arch at a principal location in the nation's capital indicates how far (the government) ​must stretch to justify this project," US District ‌Judge Tanya Chutkan said, issuing Friday's order.

Chutkan has directed the government to provide a status report on Monday to ensure its compliance with the order.

On Thursday, the National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC) gave its approval to the arch project in an 8-4 vote, which came after a nine-and-a-half-hour hearing that saw dozens of witnesses express their opposition to the construction and question both its legality and purpose.

The building of a triumphal arch in Washington D.C. to mark the 250th anniversary of the US Declaration of Independence on July 4, was first floated as an idea by Trump last year.

In April this year, Trump confirmed that the plans for the arch had been filed with the US Commission of Fine Arts.

The arch draws inspiration from the Arc de Triomphe in Paris but would be over 50% taller than the famous French monument.

The proposed site for the project has drawn criticism. The towering structure, across the Potomac River, would lie between Arlington National Cemetery —  the final resting place for hundreds of thousands of US service members — and the 100-foot-tall Lincoln Memorial.

Critics say the arch would cast a shadow on graves at the hallowed cemetery. The Trump administration says it would honor veterans.

Concerns had also been raised about the project's impact on traffic.

Chutkan said on Friday that an approval would result in construction for nearly three years "that will ​disrupt traffic, create ‌noise, result in large-scale excavation, and more."

Last Saturday, the state of Virginia and the District of Columbia had sued the National Park Service and the Department of the Interior, seeking to prevent ​work from beginning on the arch and calling it "legally indefensible."

#302. Kalshi court losses pile up as judges refuse to block state gambling laws

Kalshi can’t avoid gambling law by claiming it doesn’t offer gambling, state AG says.

Kalshi is having a bad week in the federal court system. Two circuit appeals courts rejected the prediction market’s latest attempts to block state gambling laws in Connecticut, New York, and Nevada. Kalshi is separately facing a new lawsuit filed by the Arkansas attorney general.

In all cases involving Kalshi and state governments around the US, the main issue is whether state gambling laws apply to prediction markets despite Kalshi’s claim that its platform offers “swaps” that can only be regulated by the US Commodity Futures Exchange (CFTC). The Trump administration is on Kalshi’s side, with Donald Trump Jr. serving as an advisor to Kalshi in exchange for a generous equity deal.

“Kalshi insists that its products are not gambling,” but “Arkansas law is concerned with substance, not semantics,” Arkansas Attorney General Tim Griffin said yesterday when announcing his lawsuit against Kalshi. Kalshi’s prediction market lets customers “wager money on the outcome of just about anything” despite the fact that “gambling on an unregulated platform is squarely prohibited by Arkansas law,” he said.

Griffin’s lawsuit was filed in an Arkansas state court. Kalshi violated state law by offering gambling to people as young as 18 and by failing to pay taxes or comply with other restrictions, Griffin said. Arkansas law permits gambling within certain limits, such as an age minimum of 21 years old for electronic wagering accounts.

“Instead of obtaining the licenses, submitting to the oversight, complying with the restrictions, and paying the taxes required of lawful gambling operators in Arkansas, Kalshi opened its platforms to Arkansas consumers, including individuals as young as 18 years old, encouraged them to wager real money on sporting and entertainment events, and profited from those wagers,” Griffin said.

Arkansas filed its lawsuit about a week after Utah Attorney General Derek Brown lodged criminal charges against Kalshi and its founders for violating Utah’s ban on gambling. A federal judge in Utah previously ruled that Utah can enforce its anti-gambling laws against Kalshi.

Kalshi said in response to Arkansas’ lawsuit that it should not have to comply with different laws in each US state. “Kalshi is a federally regulated financial exchange,” Kalshi said in a statement provided to Ars. “Markets can’t operate when the rules change at every state line, which is why Congress created a single federal regulator, with nationwide rules. Kalshi follows those rules and will defend against Arkansas’s baseless claims.”

Many other states are trying to enforce their gambling laws against Kalshi, and the Supreme Court may ultimately decide whether they are able to do so. Kalshi has won some rulings, but Griffin may feel emboldened by the company’s recent court losses. For example, the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit ruled in August that Nevada can stop the prediction market from allowing sports bets. A panel of three judges unanimously found that sports bets on Kalshi are not swaps and can be regulated under state gambling laws.

Kalshi sought to overturn the judges’ panel ruling by seeking a rehearing in front of the entire Ninth Circuit appeals court, which has 29 judges. None of the judges supported a rehearing.

“The full court has been advised of the petition for rehearing en banc and no judge has requested a vote on whether to rehear the matter en banc,” the court said in a ruling yesterday. “The petition for panel rehearing and the petition for rehearing en banc are denied.”

Kalshi also lost on Tuesday in the Second Circuit, where it was trying to overturn earlier losses to New York and Connecticut. Kalshi sought preliminary injunctions to prevent New York and Connecticut from enforcing their gambling laws, but both requests were rejected by US district court judges.

A plaintiff seeking a preliminary injunction must show that it is likely to succeed on the merits of its case, and judges decided that Kalshi had not done so. The Second Circuit appeals court considered Kalshi’s losses to New York and Connecticut in a single case and upheld the lower-court decisions.

“Appellants have failed to make the required showing that an injunction pending appeal is warranted,” a three-judge panel ruled on Tuesday. The judges also refused to overturn Coinbase’s loss against Connecticut in a case that presented the same legal issues.

Kalshi lost another significant case in September when an appeals court determined that Ohio and Tennessee can enforce their gambling laws against the prediction market. A three-judge panel in the US Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit ruled unanimously against Kalshi in that one.

The Trump administration is simultaneously pursuing litigation against states trying to enforce gambling laws against prediction markets. The CFTC, claiming sole authority to regulate platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket, has sued Arizona, Connecticut, Illinois, Kentucky, Minnesota, New Mexico, New York, Rhode Island, Utah, and Wisconsin.

Kalshi’s biggest win came in April in the Third Circuit, where the appeals court ruled that New Jersey cannot regulate sports bets on prediction markets. Judges there decided that wagers on Kalshi meet the federal definition of swaps, defined under US law as contracts in which payment “is dependent on the occurrence, nonoccurrence, or the extent of the occurrence of an event or contingency associated with a potential financial, economic, or commercial consequence.”

“Kalshi’s sports-related event contracts are swaps traded on a CFTC-licensed DCM [designated contract market], so the CFTC has exclusive jurisdiction,” Third Circuit judges wrote.

But other courts that ruled against Kalshi found that at least some kinds of wagers on the prediction market are not swaps and that US law allows regulation of prediction markets by both state and federal governments. New Jersey asked the Supreme Court to reverse its loss in the Third Circuit, and 39 other states and the District of Columbia filed a brief supporting New Jersey’s petition.

#301. iPhone Duo just got a new accessibility feature in iOS 27.3 beta

Reachability helps make it easier to use the foldable with one hand.

Apple this week deployed the latest beta builds of its operating systems, including one for iOS 27.3. Along with a redesigned Health app and a slew of new Siri AI actions for various apps, the beta includes a useful accessibility feature for the iPhone Duo.

If you have Apple's first foldable, the reachability function should make it easier to use the device with one hand. If you swipe outwards from either edge on the exterior display, iOS will slide everything on the screen closer to your thumb, as MacRumors noted. For instance, if you're using your iPhone Duo with your right hand, you might pull your browser over to the side so you can more easily tap the back button, which is typically on the left of the screen.

You can enable reachability in the Settings app. Go to Accessibility > Touch and then you can toggle on the feature from there.

Reachability isn't exactly a new option on Apple devices. The company first deployed it on the iPhone 6 all the way back in 2014 to make it easier to use phones with larger displays (for what it's worth, the iPhone 5 is still my favorite model, largely because of the screen size). On most iPhones, reachability pulls what's on the screen downwards rather than to the side. Still, it's a welcome addition to the iPhone Duo, which has a 5.4-inch OLED display on the outside.

You can ask Claude to look through your accounts to spot unexpected fees, double-charges and any monthly bills that have gone up over the year. It can also generate weekly spending charts, expense calendars and budget breakdowns. And if there are any terms you're not familiar with, like say APR, you can ask Claude to explain those too.

Looking forward, Anthropic says it's exploring how Claude can work alongside licensed professionals and regulated firms to offer financial advice. Just what that might look like, the company doesn't say, but it's asking that banks and wealth managers get in touch. The timing of today's announcement probably has a lot to do with Anthropic's impending IPO, which the company is expected to complete sometime in the next few weeks.

#298. Software squeezes more data out of Webb Telescope for imaging exoplanets

Software optimizes a physical model of the telescope to reduce noise.

With a huge and still-growing catalog of exoplanets, researchers are eager to take the next steps: trying to infer what conditions are like on them, either by imaging them directly or by capturing the light that has passed through their atmosphere. Both are substantial challenges, given the presence of stars that are far, far brighter than light that has come to us via the planet.

While telescopes can be fitted with devices called coronagraphs that block out much of a star’s light, there are limits to their effectiveness, caused by noise from subtle variations in the telescope’s configuration and pointing between observations. Now, researchers have developed a new software package that optimizes a physical model of the telescope in a way that allows us to better model these differences, producing low-noise imaging of exoplanets.

Central to this work is the concept of a point spread function. If you use a telescope to image a single point of light, it will not appear that way in the actual image. Instead, it will be slightly blurry and spread out, due to imperfections in the telescope hardware and the limits of our ability to keep it pointed accurately through the time it takes to image something. The mathematical description of how a telescope distorts a point of light is called its point spread function.

There are two ways to figure out what the point spread function is. One is to use the telescope to image a known target and use those observations to derive a mathematical description of the point spread function. This is effective at reducing noise but has its limits, as the behavior of the telescope hardware can change over time, and the point spread function may vary with the wavelengths being imaged.

The alternative is to try to model the hardware’s behavior and use that model to derive a point spread function. But modern telescopes are incredibly complicated instruments, with many, many factors feeding into their performance in ways that can be difficult to ascertain, even with the full engineering schematics. As a result, these models simply contain too many parameters that need to be tuned to make this route computationally tractable.

But anyone paying attention to the world of AI developments will recognize that we’ve become quite successful at tuning billions of parameters in neural networks, in part through a mathematical technique called gradient descent. And, because this is central to training large neural networks, people have put a lot of work into optimizing the performance of gradient descent on GPUs.

So a team of researchers has developed a process they’re calling FLIP (a non-acronym for Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets) that uses a physical model of the hardware (in this case, the NIRCam on the James Webb Space Telescope) with 106 possible parameters, and then uses software to optimize all its parameters. The optimization starts with a simulated point spread function, then uses gradient descent to optimize its performance on data from an actual star. Run on a current GPU, this process only takes a bit more than half an hour.

The researchers then fine-tune the results on the actual scientific image they are analyzing. This last part of the process is critical, since some variables will differ between observations.

To test how this works, the researchers used observations of two stars with known exoplanets (HIP 65426 and 51 Eridani), along with a third (TYC 5899) that doesn’t have any known exoplanets but is known to vary a lot between observations. These are young stars, and two of them have massive planets that are still warm from their gravitational collapse, allowing them to have been imaged previously.

Using Webb data, the team used FLIP to boost the signal-to-noise ratio by a factor of 1.5 to 2, depending on the observations. At a wavelength that can be used to detect carbon dioxide, they were able to spot one of the planets in the Webb data for the first time. For TYC 5899, the approach boosted the sensitivity of the observations by a factor of 15.

The researchers point out that the applications go beyond getting a better view of known planets. By lowering the noise, it should also be possible to spot dimmer (and hence older or lower-mass) ones that had previously eluded detection. They also think they can modify FLIP to highlight where it’s making the most dramatic changes to the model, which can potentially tell us useful things about what’s going on with the telescope’s hardware.

Nature, 2026. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11213-z (About DOIs).

Assembly Bill 1709 demands that platforms remove "psychologically exploitative features."

Google, Meta and TikTok are suing to block a recent California law that's intended to protect kids from some of the more harmful aspects of social media, according to Reuters. Assembly Bill 1709 is part of a larger package that Governor Gavin Newsom introduced earlier this year and it prohibits social media platforms from offering underage kids "psychologically exploitative features" that could lead to compulsive use.

This includes stuff like sending videos through autoplay and giving children under 16 personalized recommendations. The three social media giants say this is in violation of the First Amendment and Section 230 of the federal Communications Decency Act, which has often been used to shield tech companies from liability.

The three companies filed separate suits at various courts throughout California. "The state cannot, consistent with the First Amendment, override Meta's editorial judgments," Meta wrote in its complaint. Google and TikTok made similar arguments.

Newsom said when he signed the law that children's safety should always come first when considering social media platforms in California. The state "will not stand by while unregulated technology puts our children at risk," he noted.

While many disagree on the potential solution, there's not much of an argument to be made regarding the severity of the problem. TikTok, Meta and Google are currently fighting thousands of lawsuits by individuals, school districts, cities and government entities that all claim that social media platforms addict children and have caused a mental health crisis. To that end, many states regulate children's access to social media.

Today's lawsuits are still in the early stages. We'll update you as they make their way through the California court system.

#295. 2023 March Madness: Will UConn or San Diego State triumph in the national championship game that 'means everything?'

The University of Connecticut won its fifth men’s basketball national title with a 76-59 victory over San Diego State University on Monday night at NRG Stadium in Houston.

Senior guard Tristen Newton led UConn (31-8) with 19 points and 10 rebounds while Final Four Most Outstanding Player Adama Sanogo, a junior forward, chipped in with 17 points and 10 rebounds.

“We weren’t ranked going into the year so we had the chip on our shoulder,” UConn head coach Dan Hurley told game broadcaster CBS. “We knew the level that we could play at, even through those dark times,” he added, referencing the team’s six losses in eight games during the regular season.

He said going into the tournament his group had confidence garnered during the season.

“And when you have the type of leaders like Andre Jackson (game-high six assists Monday) and Adama Sanogo, they kept this team together, got us back on track and we knew we were the best team in the tournament going in and we just had to play to our level,” he added.

San Diego State (32-7) was topped by Keshad Johnson who had 14 points.

UConn trailed very early but San Diego State was undone by an 11-minute, eight-second stretch in which they scored just five free throws and missed 12 consecutive shots from the field. The Huskies went from down 10-6 to up 36-24 at halftime.

The Aztecs made a run midway through the second half and narrowed the deficit to five at 60-55 with 5:19 to play but the Huskies scored the next nine to take a comfortable lead into the final two minutes.

“We battled. Battled back to five in the second half, but gave them too much separation,” San Diego State coach Brian Dutcher said. “We had to be at our best. We weren’t at our best. A lot had to do with UConn.”

Senior guard Adam Seiko told reporters they gave themselves a chance with their second half comeback but UConn “just made a little bit more plays” at the end.

“They have a lot of weapons. They were pretty good,” said Matt Bradley, also a senior guard. “To beat them, we had to make shots. I shot poorly. And you had to have a really good game to beat those dudes on the offensive end.”

UConn won each of its six tournament games by at least 10 points, with its closest game being a 13-point win over the University of Miami in the national semifinals.

“I just want to thank my teammates, my coaches who believed in me. If it were not for them I would not be here right now,” Sanogo told CBS.

Jordan Hawkins, who scored 16 points for UConn, talked about winning the crown one day after his cousin, Angel Reese of Louisiana State University, won the women’s title.

“I mean it’s absolutely amazing that we both get this opportunity and I mean the family reunion is going to be great so that’s all I know,” he said.

UConn enters rarefied air as only the sixth team to win five NCAA men’s basketball championships, joining UCLA (11), Kentucky (eight), North Carolina (six), Duke (five) and Indiana (five). All of UConn’s titles have come since 1999 with the most recent before Monday occurring in 2014.

UConn’s women’s teams have won 11 basketball national titles.

CNN’s Steve Almasy and Issy Ronald contributed to this report.

#294. BMW bumps battery for the better: The 2027 i7 60 xDrive, driven

BMW has updated its flagship sedan with the newest EV and infotainment tech.

When BMW debuted the new 7 Series in 2022, it set a new standard for large luxury sedans, increasingly irrelevant though that class is. Rather than siloing off an electric alternative like Mercedes, with its EQS alongside the normal S-Class, BMW simply made the powertrain an option. Stick with a V8 if you want, or consider the rather good electric version instead—only subtle differences like the badging and lack of exhaust pipes give the game away.

Since then, BMW has brought out a string of even newer electric vehicles for the 5 and 3 Series (plus their SUV counterparts). It has switched from battery packs made of prismatic cells to more energy-dense arrangements of cylindrical cells. The motors are still electrically excited synchronous ones, but now the drive units feature silicon carbide inverters and more compact packaging.

This sixth-generation electric powertrain was designed for the clean-sheet Neue Klasse family, which also threw out the legacy cruft of dozens and dozens of discrete single-function electronic control units for a handful of powerful domain controllers. These computers take over those functions but with much faster processing power—and therefore more capabilities in terms of chassis control or powertrain efficiency—as well as the ability to be more easily updated.

Which could have left BMW with something of a problem—should the flagship be clearly outclassed in terms of power and energy density and range efficiency by, well, all the other EVs in the range? Clearly, the board decided the answer to that was no, and for the 7 Series’ midlife update, the i7 got some comprehensive surgery under the skin.

Compared to the last i7 I drove, the 2027 model boasts a higher-capacity battery pack, now 112.5 kWh (net) up from 101.7 kWh, although BMW stuck with a 400 V architecture, unlike in the Neue Klasse or the iX5 we recently drove. A less-powerful 50 xDrive and a more powerful M70 xDrive will also be available, but at the first drive, I sampled the midrange 60 xDrive model, which features a combined 544 hp (400 KW) and 549 lb-ft (745 Nm), roughly equivalent to the pre-facelift car.

Despite that power and torque, the i7 60 doesn’t feel fast like a Porsche Taycan might, and you won’t want to hustle it down a mountain road the way you might the Porsche. The entire driving experience is waftier than that, with the car offering more of a magic carpet ride, a la the iX SUV or even that very fancy cousin of the i7, the Rolls-Royce Spectre.

Even with launch control, 0–60 mph takes 4.6 seconds. Once upon a time, this would have been considered excellent—the V12 750i of the mid-1990s needed at least two seconds more to do that job. But 30 years later, electric sedans from Lucid and Tesla and Porsche and a whole load of Chinese automakers will get you there in less than half the i7’s time, should you want that. If you’re looking for an outright speed machine that will rearrange your internal organs under acceleration, look elsewhere.

In fact, the i7 was remarkably relaxed; even with the traction and stability control turned down, it refused to chirp a wheel or even threaten to break loose in the dry at speeds considered acceptable on the road. But drive it in a more relaxed manner, and it rewards. The steering is precise, and it coasts beautifully on flat or downhill grades, a consequence of those EESMs that offer no resistance to the road when they’re not receiving a charge. The same very smooth regenerative braking to a stop that we experienced in the iX3 and iX5 shows up in the i7, too.

First drive events are never a good way to determine range efficiency, but BMW says between 344—362 miles depending on wheel size. With only a 400 V pack, DC fast-charging tops out at 250 kW (up from 195 kW), and a 10–80 percent charge takes about 28 minutes. Like other model-year 2027 BMW EVs, the i7 has a NACS charging port.

The domain controller for the powertrain also helps efficiency by working with the route-planning software. BMW also runs AI simulations of the battery based on previous charging cycles when planning routes and picking charging stops along the destination and will even take the cost per kWH at different stations into account.

There was also some rather radical surgery in the cabin, with BMW’s new Panoramic iDrive screen running along the base of the windshield, and its new trapezoidal infotainment touchscreen replacing the older system that was inspired by boutique hotel interiors.

BMW also put in a new domain controller for the infotainment systems. The front passenger screen and theater screen that folds down from the roof for the rear passengers operate independently of each other and the main infotainment screen—logging in to YouTube or Disney+ on one will not log you in on the others, for instance. Watching content on the theater screen in the back is also a little more enticing in the abstract than the practical.

The 31.3-inch touchscreen boasts 8K resolution, but because of the aspect ratio of the screen, if you’re watching a movie—or perhaps F1 qualifying—it will only fill the middle third of the screen, with big black bars on either side. Plus, you have to tilt your head back quite a bit to look up at the screen. The Dolby Atmos sound system was impressive to my relatively cloth ears, though.

While BMW has increased the processing power, there was still some noticeable lag on the main infotainment screen. The Alexa-based voice recognition software was notably better than when I encountered it a few months ago in the iX3, however.

The new i7 range starts at $106,200 for the 50 xDrive, or $124,700 for the 60 xDrive.

#293. The FAA is finally phasing out floppy disks from air traffic control

The US Federal Aviation Administration is getting some probably overdue upgrades. The flight agency announced today that it is modernizing some air traffic control systems that have to date been running on floppy disks. You read that right: floppy disks.

For those of you too young to remember, floppy disks were precursors to CDs as a means of storing and running digital data, particularly computer files and programs. IBM developed the first one back in 1971. The FAA systems in question date back to the 1980s. Unsurprisingly, the bulletin from the agency says the coming upgrades will give air traffic controllers faster access to information, reduce repair expenses and improve safety for public air travel.

The FAA's diskette systems contain "vital weather and other critical information" for air traffic controllers, and they're still in use at more than 400 facilities around the country. They'll be replaced by a more modern system called Enterprise – Information Display System (E-IDS), which is comprised of a digital display for relaying status information, updates and other alerts to air traffic teams. The FAA plans to have E-IDS installed in 435 sites by the end of 2028; the first five locations to receive the upgrades are the Atlantic City International Airport, Nashville International Airport and Greater Rochester International Airport, as well as data processing hubs in Atlanta and Salt Lake City.

Despite the age of floppy disk tech, they've actually remained more common in government systems than you might expect. The US Air Force only just ended its use of 8-inch diskettes tied to nuclear missile launch silos in 2019. The Japanese government announced in 2024 that it had phased out all but one of its systems that still relied on floppy disks.

Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam have asked the Supreme Court for bail once more, having spent over six years in jail. Elsewhere, the top court has clarified when the 24-hour clock for producing an arrested person starts.

Here is a roundup of the biggest headlines from across India on Friday, November 6.

Delhi's air edged toward the "severe" category on Friday, two days before Diwali. The overall Air Quality Index (AQI) stood at 391, and 30 of the city's 59 monitoring stations were already in the severe band, news agency PTI reported. India's pollution board classifies readings above 400 as severe.

A government-backed early-warning system expects severe air quality from Friday through the major festival of Diwali on Sunday. Mahesh Palawat of Skymet told PTI that weakening winds could trap pollutants from Monday.

The Supreme Court took up the crisis Friday in a case on pollution in the capital region. Chief Justice Surya Kant opened by saying: "I hope you all are enjoying the weather in Delhi," local media reported.

The bench pointed to vehicles as a major cause. "Look at the roads in Delhi. Look at the roads connecting Delhi to Noida… the kind of bumper-to-bumper traffic… That's the major cause," the court said.

The chief justice added that "AQI is already touching 400."

Amicus curiae Aparajita Singh told the court that breathing the region's air is like smoking 30 cigarettes a day and that crop burning in nearby states accounts for 14% of Delhi's pollution.

India wants to become one of the world's leading artificial intelligence (AI) powers by 2047. Both opportunities and challenges lie ahead on the path to achieving that goal.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

India's Supreme Court has ruled that police must bring a person before a magistrate within 24 hours of first detaining them, not 24 hours from when an arrest is formally recorded, local media reported.

The constitution requires anyone held by police to be presented to a magistrate within a day. Reports suggest that police have often kept people in informal "detention" for hours or even days before logging an arrest, which delays that clock.

Justices Ujjal Bhuyan and Atul S. Chandurkar criticized the practice as unconstitutional.

"An artificial distinction between 'arrest' and 'detention' would be highly problematic," the court said, as reported by Live Law.

The case had been brought to the court after four people were detained for some 18 hours before formally being arrested. The Supreme Court ordered their immediate release.

Going forward, anyone held beyond 24 hours without being brought before a magistrate must be freed, and only travel time to court may be excluded, the court ruled.

Magistrates must record when a person was actually detained and may refuse to extend custody if the detention has been unreasonably long. The court ordered the judgment be sent to state police chiefs.

National Human Rights Commission data show 11,656 deaths in police or jail custody between 2016 and 2022, the Telegraph reported.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Activists Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam approached the Supreme Court on Thursday for bail once again in the 2020 Delhi riots "larger conspiracy" case.

They are challenging a September 30 Delhi High Court order that rejected their pleas, Bar and Bench reported. The pleas had not yet been listed for hearing.

The High Court held that judicial discipline bound it to the Supreme Court's January 5 order and that it could not alter the terms set there. In that order, the top court refused bail to the two while granting relief to five co-accused, saying they "stand on a qualitatively different footing as compared to other accused," local media reported.

The ruling allowed them to reapply once the protected witnesses had been examined or a year had passed, whichever came first.

Imam says he has spent six years and nine months in jail as an undertrial without the prosecution examining any of its 47 protected witnesses, Live Law reported. He argues the witness condition is therefore unlikely to be met in time.

The pleas also say over 900 witnesses are yet to be examined and that continued imprisonment violates the right to life and liberty under Article 21.

On May 18, another Supreme Court bench criticized the January order, observing that "bail is the rule and jail is an exception" even under the anti-terror law UAPA.

Delhi Police have described the two as "masterminds" of the violence that took place in February 2020. However, nearly seven years later, the trial has not yet begun.

This is Seerat from DW's Studio Delhi. The lights are up and sweets are out as the city gears up for the festive season. But a resurgence of the toxic winter air is truly killing the vibe.
